findings.title: tokio 1.52.3 is affected by RUSTSEC-2026-0386 (no severity rating)

The advisory carries neither a CVSS vector nor a database severity, so QSI rates it low and preliminary until it is triaged. None of the affected functions (tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::new, tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::try_new, tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::try_with_interest, tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::with_interest) is named in the audited code: the advisory does not apply unless they are reached indirectly (traits, macros, other dependencies).

findings.description: OSV.dev lists 1 advisories (0 rated high or critical) for 1 crates.io package(s) that only development or build tooling pulls in (Cargo.lock): e.g. scc@2.4.0 [dev]: RUSTSEC-2026-0205. The manifests mark them as such (devDependencies, "dev": true in package-lock.json, pnpm importers sections, [dev-dependencies]/[build-dependencies] reached through Cargo.lock, or — for yarn.lock, which records no scope at all — package.json reached through the lock graph), so they are not part of what ships.
findings.impact: They do not reach users of the product. They can affect developer machines and CI (supply chain): a compromised or vulnerable tool can tamper with builds.
findings.recommendation: Update the tooling during routine maintenance; prioritise packages that run in CI with secrets or that produce release artefacts.
findings.retest: Re-run the dependency scan after updating.
findings.limitations: Advisory data comes from OSV.dev at the recorded time. Scopes come from the manifests; a registry crate's own build dependencies cannot be told apart in Cargo.lock, so the runtime set may be larger than reality, never smaller.
findings.method: OSV.dev querybatch lookup of exact versions; scope from devDependencies, package-lock.json dev flags, pnpm importers sections, the Cargo.lock graph rooted at the Cargo.toml tables, and — for yarn.lock, which records no scope — the lock graph walked from package.json. Where a runtime requirement cannot be resolved in a lock, that lock is left unclassified rather than risking a package being set aside wrongly.
findings.repro: Look the packages listed in the evidence up at https://osv.dev and check their scope in Cargo.lock.

pq.assumptions: Planning assumptions: x for key establishment, x for signatures, y are the defaults of the risk profile “Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet”, not the client's figures; with the client's actual lifetimes the verdict can change.

roles.label: transaction and message signing
roles.action: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them

roles.label: role not determined
roles.action: Classify each usage, record data lifetimes, and plan migration to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), in a hybrid/composite form where the ecosystem supports it; introduce an abstraction layer for crypto-agility

maturity.label: post-quantum in use outside the critical paths
maturity.next: Extend post-quantum protection to the critical roles that stay classical, starting with what can be recorded today (wrapped keys, channel key exchange).
facts: A post-quantum library is declared as a dependency

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.

references.title: A. Chailloux, M. Naya-Plasencia, A. Schrottenloher — An Efficient Quantum Collision Search Algorithm and Implications on Symmetric Cryptography (ASIACRYPT 2017; IACR ePrint 2017/847)
references.status: peer-reviewed article: Õ(2^{2n/5}) time, O(n) qubits, Õ(2^{n/5}) classical memory

references.title: C. Chevignard, P.-A. Fouque, A. Schrottenloher — Reducing the Number of Qubits in Quantum Discrete Logarithms on Elliptic Curves (IACR ePrint 2026/280)
references.status: revision of a EUROCRYPT 2026 paper: 3.12n + o(n) qubits; for n = 256, 1193 qubits and 22 runs of 2^38.98 Toffoli gates

references.title: C. Zalka — Grover's quantum searching algorithm is optimal (Phys. Rev. A 60, 2746, 1999; arXiv:quant-ph/9711070)
references.status: peer-reviewed article: optimal for any success probability; parallel search gains no more than splitting the space

references.title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System v3.1: Specification Document
D. J. Bernstein — Cost analysis of hash collisions: Will quantum computers make SHARCS obsolete? (2009)
D. Litinski — How to compute a 256-bit elliptic curve private key with only 50 million Toffoli gates (arXiv:2306.08585)
references.status: preprint (2023-06-14): 6000 modules × 1152 physical qubits, one key per 10 minutes under its architecture assumptions

references.title: FIPS 205 — Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA)
G. Brassard, P. Høyer, A. Tapp — Quantum Algorithm for the Collision Problem (LATIN '98; arXiv:quant-ph/9705002)
references.status: peer-reviewed article: collisions of r-to-one functions in O((N/r)^{1/3}) expected evaluations

references.title: J. Proos, C. Zalka — Shor's discrete logarithm quantum algorithm for elliptic curves (Quantum Inf. Comput. 3(4), 2003; arXiv:quant-ph/0301141)
L. K. Grover — A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search (STOC 1996)
M. Amy et al. — Estimating the cost of generic quantum pre-image attacks on SHA-2 and SHA-3 (SAC 2016; arXiv:1603.09383)
references.status: peer-reviewed article: SHA-256 about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits; SHA3-256 about 2^146.5 cycles on 2^20

references.title: M. Cain et al. — Shor's algorithm is possible with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits (arXiv:2603.28627)
references.status: preprint (2026-03-30): P-256 in a few days with 26,000 physical neutral-atom qubits; RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude longer

references.title: M. Mosca — Cybersecurity in an Era with Quantum Computers: Will We Be Ready? (IEEE Security & Privacy, 2018)
references.status: peer-reviewed article; source of the x + y > z migration inequality

references.title: M. Roetteler, M. Naehrig, K. Svore, K. Lauter — Quantum resource estimates for computing elliptic curve discrete logarithms (ASIACRYPT 2017)
references.status: peer-reviewed article: at most 9n + 2⌈log2 n⌉ + 10 qubits and 448 n^3 log2 n + 4090 n^3 Toffoli gates

references.title: NIST IR 8547 — Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
references.status: final (2026-10-27; the initial public draft of November 2024 is obsoleted). Tables 2 and 4: ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA signatures, finite-field and elliptic-curve DH and MQV, and RSA key establishment are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035 at every key size — the draft deprecated only the 112-bit level. A composite (hybrid) key establishment stays FIPS 140-validatable while one input comes from an approved scheme. Repeats the federal deadlines of OMB M-26-15: post-quantum key establishment by 2030-12-31 and signatures by 2031-12-31 for high value assets and high impact systems

references.title: NIST — Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization: Evaluation Criteria, Security (Call for Proposals, Section 4.A.5)
references.status: security categories: AES-128 key search 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates, AES-192 2^233/MAXDEPTH, AES-256 2^298/MAXDEPTH; MAXDEPTH 2^40–2^96

references.title: OSV.dev — open-source vulnerability database and API
